did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah’s vision opens by giving a historical date: the year King Uzziah died. In the vision, Isaiah sees the Lord seated on a high and exalted throne, and the hem of his robe fills the temple.
Did you know? The seraphim are described as having six wings: with two they cover their faces, with two they cover their feet, and with two they fly.
Did you know? The seraphim call to one another, “Holy, holy, holy,” declaring that the glory of the Lord fills the whole earth.
Did you know? The sound of the seraphim’s voices shakes the doorposts—the frames or pillars of the entrances—and the temple fills with smoke.

Did you know? Encountering this vision of holiness leads Isaiah to recognize his sin and the uncleanness of his lips. He also emphasizes that the people among whom he lives are described as a people of unclean lips.
Did you know? One of the seraphim takes a burning coal from the altar with tongs. This describes the source of the means by which Isaiah’s mouth will be purified.
Did you know? After the seraph touches Isaiah’s lips, he tells him, “Your guilt is taken away, and your sin is atoned for.” The purification prepares Isaiah for his prophetic mission.
Did you know? When Isaiah hears the question, “Whom shall I send?” he immediately answers, “Here I am. Send me!” His response expresses his willingness to accept the mission.

Did you know? Isaiah’s mission includes a difficult message: the people will hear but not understand, and see but not know. The prophecy describes a state of spiritual insensitivity to the words of warning.

Did you know? Even after the prophecy describes desolation and destruction, a note of hope remains: a tenth will survive, and ultimately a “holy seed” will remain from it, like the stump left by the terebinth and the oak after their leaves have fallen.
